planting.note: Surface-sow seed in spring into constantly saturated, loamy or clay soil; division of rooted mat sections is faster and more reliable than seed.

directions: Forming a mossy, mat-like groundcover of rounded leaves studded with tiny bright yellow snapdragon-like flowers, this species makes an excellent lawn-alternative or living mulch at the edge of a pond or bog garden. It wants constantly saturated, loamy or clay soil and struggles in sandy or fast-draining sites, performing best where seep water or pond overflow keeps the surface wet year-round. Because it spreads by creeping stolons rather than by height, use it as a living carpet along boggy path edges or wet meadow margins rather than a border plant.

planting.note: Surface-sow seed or divide rhizome clumps in spring at a snowmelt-fed streamlet, alpine bog, or the cool side of a rock garden with permanently moist, gravelly soil.

directions: A cold-hardy, rhizomatous alpine and subalpine perennial for high-elevation rock gardens and mountain-stream features, this species tolerates colder, higher sites than the more familiar common yellow monkeyflower while carrying similarly large, showy yellow flowers. It benefits from cool root zones even in summer, so mulch or shade the crown if growing it at lower, warmer elevations. Established rhizome mats can be lifted and divided every two to three years to maintain vigor and prevent overcrowding.

planting.note: Sow seed or root softwood cuttings in fall into lean, fast-draining soil under native oaks; withhold summer irrigation once rooted in.

directions: A drought-adapted, evergreen-ish subshrub unusual among monkeyflowers for tolerating true dry shade, this species carries ruffled, azalea-like creamy white to pale lavender flowers over a long late-spring-to-fall season. Plant in lean, fast-draining soil and site it specifically to exploit its dry-shade tolerance — it is one of the few monkeyflowers that will flower well beneath an oak canopy once established. Expect semi- to full summer dormancy with foliage flush returning at the first fall rains; a light shearing after the main bloom flush keeps growth dense rather than leggy.

planting.note: Scatter seed directly onto bare mineral soil in fall and let winter rains do the germinating; leave the site dry and undisturbed through summer.

directions: A charming miniature annual for rock gardens and serpentine-soil native plant displays, this species carries tiny magenta, gold-and-purple-striped flowers in very early spring when little else is blooming. It is a specialist for the toughest, most nutrient-poor garden sites, having evolved to thrive on nutrient-poor serpentine barrens where competing vegetation can't establish. Grow it in a scree bed, serpentine or decomposed-granite rock garden, or shallow container where its near-invisible stature can be appreciated up close.

planting.note: Surface-sow seed in spring at stream edges, seeps, or springs in sandy or gravelly soil, giving the sprawling stems room to scramble over a boulder or pond liner edge.

directions: An easy, fast, sprawling-to-climbing annual with a very wide native range from British Columbia to South Dakota to northern Mexico, this species makes an adaptable rain-garden or seep filler with small yellow flowers appearing in great profusion over a long season. Its sprawling, somewhat sticky stems scramble over rocks or neighboring low plants rather than stand upright, so give it room to spill. It self-sows readily where moisture is dependable and tolerates more shade than most of its yellow-flowered relatives.

planting.note: Direct-sow onto bare scree, decomposed granite, or disturbed gravel in fall; rich, mulched beds will outcompete it.

directions: A striking reddish-purple-flowered annual adapted to bare, disturbed mineral substrates like rockslides and scree, this species is ideal for a gravel garden or green roof where most annuals won't compete well. It attracts an unusually wide range of native bees. Direct-sow in fall and let the plant complete its entire life cycle during the wet season; the reddish-purple flowers with yellow-spotted throats are showiest in cool spring weather and fade once the dry season sets in.

planting.note: Sow seed in fall or very early spring, surface-sown or lightly pressed in, into lean, rocky soil in full sun; keep seedlings consistently moist through their short life cycle.

directions: A rare, highly ornamental annual endemic to the southern Sierra Nevada and Tehachapi region, this species carries a strikingly patterned white-and-maroon-veined face, making it both a garden novelty and a conservation-minded choice since nursery-propagated seed supports ex-situ conservation of a narrowly endemic species. Replicate its open, bare, rocky, disturbed forest and woodland habitat with lean soil and full sun rather than a rich garden bed. Its boldly maroon-veined, white flowers make it a good choice for a raised rock trough or gravel bed where the intricate face pattern can be viewed up close.
